subject: Mathematics
period_schedule_display:
Period schedule:
  Row 1: 45 minutes × 11 periods = 495 minutes
Total: 11 periods · 8h 15min

periods.activity_title: Per Hundred: Naming the Fraction We Already Know

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Example 1, section 1.1 p.1
textbook_items_in_class.description: Surya mixes red and yellow paint; red makes up 3/4 of the mixture. Convert 3/4 to a percentage using equivalent fractions and two algebraic methods. Answer: 75%.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Example 2, section 1.1 p.2
textbook_items_in_class.description: Surya saves 2/5 of prize money for a canvas. Express 2/5 as a percentage using three methods (equivalent fraction, cross-multiplication, bar model). Answer: 40%.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Example 3, section 1.1 p.3
textbook_items_in_class.description: Express 24% as a fraction. Since percentage = fraction over 100, 24% = 24/100 = 12/50 = 6/25. Generalises: z% equals any fraction equivalent to z/100.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q2, section 1.1 p.3
textbook_items_in_class.description: Nandini has 25 marbles, 15 white. What percentage are white? Choose from given options (MCQ).

homework.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 1.1 p.3

time_bands.activity: Open with the question: when two biscuit brands declare '9 out of 34 g is sugar' and '13 out of 45 g is sugar', which is sweeter? Take a show of hands. Establish that comparing raw fractions with different denominators is difficult, and introduce the idea that re-expressing both over 100 dissolves the confusion — this is what 'per cent' (from the Latin per centum, out of hundred) means.

Work through Example 1, section 1.1 p.1 ("Surya mixes red and yellow paint; red makes up 3/4 of the mixture....") on the board using the equivalent-fraction method (3/4 = 75/100 = 75%). Then show the cross-multiplication method alongside. Invite students to verify both routes give the same answer. Move to Example 2, section 1.1 p.2 ("Surya saves 2/5 of prize money for a canvas....") and let pairs try the bar-model method before the class compares all three approaches.

Work through Example 3, section 1.1 p.3 ("Express 24% as a fraction....") to show the reverse conversion: percentage → fraction → simplest form. Establish the FDP link: 24% = 24/100 = 0.24. Ask: what fraction is 40%? 75%? Students write answers on slates or scraps.

Students attempt Figure it Out Q2, section 1.1 p.3 ("Nandini has 25 marbles, 15 white. What percentage are white?...") individually, then share reasoning. Emphasise that the denominator 25 scales to 100 by multiplying by 4 — a quick mental check.

Class reviews two or three student solutions for Q2. Teacher points out the connection to the biscuit comparison opened at the start: both sugar fractions can now be converted and compared. Students note Figure it Out Q1, section 1.1 p.3 ("Express six fractions as percentages: 3/5, 7/14, 9/20....") for home practice.

periods.teacher_notes: Watch for students who multiply the numerator by 100 but forget to divide by the denominator — a common slip when using the cross-multiplication template. The bar-model in Example 2, section 1.1 p.2 is particularly useful for students who find the algebraic route abstract; pair it with the equivalent-fraction method to show both paths lead to the same answer. Example 3, section 1.1 p.3 (reverse conversion) is a good self-study pointer for students who finish early.
materials: Slates or scrap paper for quick checks

periods.activity_title: Comparing and Ordering: Fractions Dressed as Percents

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q3, section 1.1 p.3
textbook_items_in_class.description: 15 of 80 students come to school by walking. What percentage come by walking?

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q4, section 1.1 p.3
textbook_items_in_class.description: Match four runners (A, B, C, D) shown at different positions on a race track to their approximate percentage completion from a given set (55%, 20%, 38%, 72%, 84%, 93%).

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q5, section 1.1 p.4
textbook_items_in_class.description: Insert >, <, or = without calculating: (i) 50% __ 5%; (ii) 5/10 __ 50%; (iii) 3/11 __ 61%; (iv) 30% __ 1/3.

time_bands.activity: Revisit the core definition established in section 1.1: percentage = fraction with denominator 100. Pose a warm-up: which is larger, 3/11 or 30%? Ask students to explain without computing, drawing on the equivalent-fraction and bar-model ideas from the conversion methods already studied.

Students work individually on Figure it Out Q3, section 1.1 p.3 ("15 of 80 students come to school by walking. What percentage...?"). Circulate and note students who scale the denominator versus those who set up a proportion. Bring two contrasting methods to the board and discuss which is faster for this denominator.

Introduce Figure it Out Q4, section 1.1 p.3 ("Match four runners to their approximate percentage completion....") as a group task. Students in pairs estimate each runner's position visually before computing. Groups share their reasoning; discuss how visual estimation connects to fraction intuition.

Class tackles Figure it Out Q5, section 1.1 p.4 ("Insert >, <, or = without calculating....") as a whole-group discussion. Each sub-item is a quick mental challenge: encourage estimation strategies — recognising 5/10 = 1/2 = 50%, or noting 3/11 is slightly more than 3/12 = 25%, far less than 61%. Students justify their symbol choices in one sentence each.

Consolidate: the teacher names a fraction (e.g., 7/20) and students call out the percentage; then the teacher names a percentage (e.g., 35%) and students name a simple fraction equivalent. This quick oral exchange cements the FDP trio and closes the section's content.

periods.teacher_notes: A frequent error in Q3 is writing 15/80 × 80 instead of 15/80 × 100; remind students that the multiplier is always 100 because we are rescaling to 'per hundred'. For Q5, students sometimes try to calculate 3/11 as a decimal and struggle — nudge them toward benchmark fractions (1/4, 1/3, 1/2) as anchor comparisons instead. Figure it Out Q1, section 1.1 p.3 (the six-fraction conversion set) is a useful self-study item for consolidating the conversion algorithm.

periods.activity_title: Finding the Part: Percentage of a Quantity

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Example 1, section 1.2 p.5
textbook_items_in_class.description: Madhu eats 120 g of 25%-sugar biscuits (30 g sugar); Madhav eats 95 g of 35%-sugar biscuits (33.25 g sugar). Multiple methods: ratio, proportional equation, unit-rate. Concludes Madhav consumed more sugar.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Example 2, section 1.2 p.7
textbook_items_in_class.description: Free-hand computation table: find 25%, 10%, 20%, 5% of values 100, 200, 50, 80, 10, 35, 287 without pen and paper, exploiting the relationships between percentages (e.g., 20% = 2 × 10%).

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 1.2 p.12
textbook_items_in_class.description: Find missing numbers using percentage bar models: (i) 20% of ? = 12 (given 100% shown); (ii) ? is 60% of 75; (iii) ? is 140% of ?, with two unknowns and bar models provided.

homework.book_ref: Figure it Out Q2, section 1.2 p.12
homework.description: Find the value and draw bar models for: (i) 25% of 160; (ii) 16% of 250; (iii) 62% of 360; (iv) 140% of 40; (v) 1% of 1 hour; (vi) 7% of 10 kg.

time_bands.activity: Pose the biscuit question from section 1.2: Madhu eats 120 g of biscuits that are 25% sugar; Madhav eats 95 g that are 35% sugar. Ask students to guess who consumed more sugar before any calculation. Record the class's guesses and reasoning on the board.

Work through Example 1, section 1.2 p.5 ("Madhu eats 120 g of 25%-sugar biscuits....") showing three methods — the ratio method, the proportional equation (y/100 × quantity), and the unit-rate approach. Students check each method reaches 30 g and 33.25 g. Revisit the class's initial guesses: who was right, and why did the higher percentage not guarantee more sugar?

Students pair up for Example 2, section 1.2 p.7 ("Free-hand computation table: find 25%, 10%, 20%, 5% of various values...."). Each pair completes the table without pen-and-paper arithmetic, using only the relationships between percentages (10% = quantity ÷ 10; 20% = 2 × 10%; 25% = quantity ÷ 4). Pairs compare answers with a neighbouring pair and reconcile differences.

Introduce Figure it Out Q1, section 1.2 p.12 ("Find missing numbers using percentage bar models....") as individual work. The bar model makes the proportional structure visible: 100% maps to the whole, and parts scale accordingly. Circulate and prompt students who are unsure of part (iii) to first identify what 1% of the whole would be.

Brief class check on Q1 answers. Preview Figure it Out Q2, section 1.2 p.12 ("Find the value and draw bar models for....") as home practice, reminding students that drawing the bar model is part of the task.

periods.teacher_notes: Students frequently apply y% of quantity as quantity ÷ y rather than (y/100) × quantity — the biscuit comparison in Example 1, section 1.2 p.5 surfaces this error quickly because the two quantities are different. The free-hand table in Example 2, section 1.2 p.7 builds the mental-arithmetic habits that make later estimation in section 1.3 fluent; do not shortcut it by allowing calculators. Example 3, section 1.2 p.8 (Zubin's grade problem with three solution methods) is a good self-study read for students who want additional method comparison.

periods.activity_title: Ratios, Quantities Greater Than 100%, and Estimation

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Example 4, section 1.2 p.9
textbook_items_in_class.description: Millet kanji: millet-to-water ratio is 2:7, so millet is 2/9 of mixture. Estimate first, then compute 2/9 × 100 = 22.22%. For 500 ml of mixture, millet = 5 × 22.22 = 111.1 ml.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Example 6, section 1.2 p.10
textbook_items_in_class.description: Kishanlal's daily sales vs. ₹5000 target: Day 1 ₹2000 = 40%, Day 2 ₹3500 = 70%, Day 3 ₹5000 = 100%, Day 4 ₹6000 = 120%. Introduces percentages greater than 100. Students compute Days 5–8.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Example 7, section 1.2 p.12
textbook_items_in_class.description: A farmer's harvest this year (650 kg) as a percentage of last year's (260 kg): 650/260 × 100 = 250%. Illustrates that 250% means 2.5 times the original.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q4, section 1.2 p.13
textbook_items_in_class.description: Insert >, <, = without computing (verify after estimating): (i) 50% of 510 vs. 50% of 515; (ii) 37% of 148 vs. 73% of 148; (iii) 29% of 43 vs. 92% of 110; (iv) 30% of 40 vs. 40% of 50; (v) 45% of 200 vs. 10% of 490; (vi) 30% of 80 vs. 24% of 64.

homework.book_ref: Figure it Out Q3, section 1.2 p.12
homework.description: Surya made 60 ml of deep orange paint with red paint making up 3/4. How much red paint was used? (Apply percentage/fraction to find a quantity.)

time_bands.activity: Pose the millet kanji question: if millet and water are in the ratio 2:7, what fraction of the mixture is millet? Students write the fraction, then estimate the percentage before computing. Collect estimates on the board to show the range of intuitions.

Work through Example 4, section 1.2 p.9 ("Millet kanji: millet-to-water ratio is 2:7....") step by step: convert ratio to fraction (2/9), estimate (~22%), then compute 2/9 × 100 = 22.22%. Extend to: for 500 ml of kanji, how much is millet? Students use the unit-rate idea: 1% = 5 ml, so 22.22% = 111.1 ml.

Introduce percentages greater than 100 via Example 6, section 1.2 p.10 ("Kishanlal's daily sales vs. ₹5000 target...."). Build the table of Days 1–4 together, then students complete Days 5–8 independently. Discuss: what does 120% mean in the context of a target? Then work through Example 7, section 1.2 p.12 ("A farmer's harvest this year as a percentage of last year's....") to show 250% = 2.5 times.

Students work in pairs on Figure it Out Q4, section 1.2 p.13 ("Insert >, <, = without computing (verify after estimating)...."). Each pair must write an estimation reason before verifying. Pairs swap papers and critique each other's reasoning.

Quick class debrief on the most contested sub-item of Q4. Assign Figure it Out Q3, section 1.2 p.12 ("Surya made 60 ml of deep orange paint with red paint making up 3/4....") for home practice as a direct application of the ratio-to-fraction-to-percentage chain.

periods.teacher_notes: Students often read a ratio a:b as the fraction a/b rather than a/(a+b); Example 4, section 1.2 p.9 is the place to correct this — insist on writing the total number of parts first. Percentages above 100 in Example 6 sometimes unsettle students who assume percentage must be 'less than the whole'; the sales-target context makes the meaning concrete and non-threatening. Example 5, section 1.2 p.10 (the cyclist's remaining distance) is a good self-study item for students seeking additional multi-method practice.

periods.activity_title: Scaling, Proportional Reasoning, and Estimation Games

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Activity: How Close Can You Get?, p.8
textbook_items_in_class.description: Students work in pairs, each choosing a number; both independently estimate the percentage equivalent of the fraction a/b (a < b) formed by the two numbers and announce answers within 5 seconds. The closer estimate wins. Played for 10 rounds to build proportional number sense.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q5, section 1.2 p.13
textbook_items_in_class.description: Fill in the blanks using scaling relationships: (i) given 30% of k = 70, find 60%, 90%, 120% of k; (ii) given 100% of m = 215, find 10%, 1%, 6%; (iii) given 90% of n = 270, find 9%, 18%, 100%; (iv) make 2 more questions for peers.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q6, section 1.2 p.13
textbook_items_in_class.description: Fill in the blanks: (i) 3 is __% of 300; (ii) __ is 40% of 4; (iii) 40 is 80% of __.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q10, section 1.2 p.13
textbook_items_in_class.description: Badminton training: warm-up:play:cool-down = 10%:80%:10% of 90 minutes. Find the duration of each activity.

homework.book_ref: Figure it Out Q12, section 1.2 p.13
homework.description: Halwa recipe for 4 people: Rava 40%, Sugar 40%, Ghee 20%. (i) Proportions remain the same for 8 people? (ii) If total weight is 2 kg, find weight of each ingredient.

time_bands.activity: Run Activity: How Close Can You Get?, p.8 ("Students work in pairs, each choosing a number; both estimate the percentage equivalent of the fraction a/b....") for 10 rapid rounds. One student in each pair calls out a numerator, the other a larger denominator; both announce their percentage estimate within 5 seconds; the closer one scores a point. After all rounds, pairs discuss which fractions were easiest and hardest to estimate — and why.

Students work individually on Figure it Out Q5, section 1.2 p.13 ("Fill in the blanks using scaling relationships...."). The key insight is that percentages of the same whole scale with the percentage: if 30% = 70, then 60% = 140 and 1% = 7/3. Students who finish parts (i)–(iii) write two new questions for a peer as part (iv) demands.

Figure it Out Q6, section 1.2 p.13 ("Fill in the blanks: 3 is __% of 300; __ is 40% of 4; 40 is 80% of __.") done as a class with students justifying each blank orally. Discuss the three distinct types of unknown: unknown percentage, unknown part, unknown whole — and how the same formula handles all three.

Pairs tackle Figure it Out Q10, section 1.2 p.13 ("Badminton training: warm-up:play:cool-down = 10%:80%:10% of 90 minutes...."). Students compute the three durations and verify they sum to 90 minutes. Discuss: what changes if the session were 60 minutes? This elastic thinking generalises the percentage relationship.

Brief share-out: one pair reads their self-created Q5(iv) problems; the class estimates answers. Assign Figure it Out Q12, section 1.2 p.13 ("Halwa recipe for 4 people....") for home practice as an application of fixed proportions across different totals.

periods.teacher_notes: The estimation game surfaces the very proportional intuitions the section is building — students who struggle with the game often have a procedural rather than relational understanding of percentage. In Q5, watch for students who find 60% by adding 70 + 70 without recognising that 30% is the unit; prompt them to find 10% first. Figure it Out Q9, section 1.2 p.13 (the coffee-berry plantation question) is a good self-study challenge for confident estimators.
materials: Optional: small score-card strips for the estimation game

periods.activity_title: Comparing Scores and Reading Labels: Percentage as a Common Scale

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Example 1, section 1.3 p.14
textbook_items_in_class.description: Eesha: English score 42/50 = 84%, Science score 70/80 = 87.5%. Resolves apparent ambiguity about which is better by converting both to percentages. Science score is higher.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Example 2, section 1.3 p.15
textbook_items_in_class.description: Know Your Contents (KYC): Two badam drink mixes (DEF: 99 g sugar in 150 g total = 66%; Zacni: unknown). Students complete a table converting ingredient weights to percentages to compare proportions.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Example 3, section 1.3 p.15
textbook_items_in_class.description: 'Population in 1991 is 165% of 1961' and 'increased by 65% from 1961 to 1991' — both mean q = 1.65p. Algebra confirms equivalence of 'is P% of' and 'increased by (P−100)%' statements.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 1.3 p.19
textbook_items_in_class.description: Shopkeeper buys a geometry box for ₹75 and sells for ₹110. Find profit margin with respect to cost.

homework.book_ref: Figure it Out Q5, section 1.3 p.19
homework.description: Petrol price was ₹60 in 2015 and ₹100 in 2025. Find percentage increase. Choose from MCQ options.

time_bands.activity: Pose the comparison challenge: Eesha scored 42 out of 50 in English and 70 out of 80 in Science. Ask students which subject she performed better in — take votes without calculation. Record the split on the board and note that raw scores can mislead when totals differ.

Work through Example 1, section 1.3 p.14 ("Eesha: English 42/50 = 84%, Science 70/80 = 87.5%....") to reveal that Science is higher. Extend to Example 2, section 1.3 p.15 ("Know Your Contents: Two badam drink mixes, DEF and Zacni....") where students complete the ingredient-percentage table to determine which drink is sweeter. Discuss: the percentage scale makes proportions from different-sized packets directly comparable.

Work through Example 3, section 1.3 p.15 ("'Population in 1991 is 165% of 1961' and 'increased by 65%' — both mean q = 1.65p...."). Students verify algebraically that the two phrasings are equivalent: if new = P% of old, then increase = (P − 100)% of old. Ask: 'If a value is 250% of original, by what percent did it increase?' Students answer with the formula.

Students work individually on Figure it Out Q1, section 1.3 p.19 ("Shopkeeper buys a geometry box for ₹75, sells for ₹110. Find profit margin...."). Confirm that profit % is computed on cost price. Discuss: why is the base always the cost price, not the selling price?

Brief class share for Q1. Students note the home-practice item Figure it Out Q5, section 1.3 p.19 ("Petrol price ₹60 in 2015 and ₹100 in 2025. Find percentage increase....") with a reminder that percentage increase = (increase ÷ original) × 100.

periods.teacher_notes: A common error is computing percentage increase as (new ÷ old) × 100 rather than ((new − old) ÷ old) × 100; Example 3, section 1.3 p.15 is a good place to sharpen the distinction between 'is P% of' and 'increased by (P−100)%'. The KYC activity in Example 2 connects to food-label reading — if the class has access to any real packet labels, even one, it makes the comparison vivid. Example 1, section 1.3 p.14 (Eesha's scores) is worth revisiting for self-study as a clean two-method comparison exercise.
materials: Optional: a food-product packet with ingredient label

periods.activity_title: Profit, Loss, Discount, and GST: Percentages in the Market

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Example 4, section 1.3 p.17
textbook_items_in_class.description: Kishanlal buys a sweater at ₹300, marks it at ₹480, sells at ₹430. Profit = ₹130 on CP of ₹300 → percentage profit = 130/300 × 100 = 43.3%. Students also find wholesaler and manufacturer profit percentages.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Example 5, section 1.3 p.17
textbook_items_in_class.description: Raghu buys rice at ₹35/kg, sells 10 kg for ₹300 (CP = ₹350). Loss = ₹50. Percentage loss = 50/350 × 100 = 14.28%.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Example 6, section 1.3 p.17
textbook_items_in_class.description: Shyamala sells a damaged vase at 18% loss on CP of ₹2650. Two methods: SP = 82% of 2650 = ₹2173; or loss amount = 18/100 × 2650 = 477, SP = 2650 − 477 = ₹2173.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q4, section 1.3 p.19
textbook_items_in_class.description: A clothing shop offers 25% discount on shirts originally priced at ₹300. How much does Anwar pay?

homework.book_ref: Figure it Out Q2, section 1.3 p.19
homework.description: Carpenter's cost for a chair is ₹475 with a desired 50% profit margin. Find the selling price.

time_bands.activity: Write three prices on the board for Kishanlal's sweater: cost price ₹300, marked price ₹480, selling price ₹430. Ask students what 'profit percentage' means and what it should be computed on. Take responses; surface the key question — why the cost price is the base.

Work through Example 4, section 1.3 p.17 ("Kishanlal buys a sweater at ₹300, marks it at ₹480, sells at ₹430....") computing profit = 130 on CP = 300, so profit % = 43.3%. Students then find the wholesaler's and manufacturer's profit percentages using the same chain. Establish the vocabulary: cost price (CP), marked price (MP), selling price (SP), discount.

Move to Example 5, section 1.3 p.17 ("Raghu buys rice at ₹35/kg, sells 10 kg for ₹300....") and Example 6, section 1.3 p.17 ("Shyamala's vase at 18% loss...."). For Example 6, show both methods: subtract the loss amount OR multiply by (100 − 18)% = 82%. Students decide which method is faster for their own mental arithmetic.

Students work individually on Figure it Out Q4, section 1.3 p.19 ("A clothing shop offers 25% discount on shirts originally priced at ₹300. How much does Anwar pay?"). Circulate; check that students subtract the discount from the marked price rather than from an unrelated base.

Class debrief on Q4. Introduce the GST context briefly: if an item costs ₹300 and attracts 18% GST, the customer pays 118% of ₹300 — a direct extension of the 'percentage of a quantity' method. Students note Figure it Out Q2, section 1.3 p.19 ("Carpenter's cost for a chair, desired 50% profit margin....") for home practice.

periods.teacher_notes: Students consistently confuse 'selling at 25% discount' with 'selling at 25% of the price'; make the subtraction explicit — SP = MP − discount amount, or equivalently SP = (100 − d)% of MP. The two-method approach in Example 6, section 1.3 p.17 is pedagogically important: the direct multiplication method (SP = 82% of CP) is faster and prepares students for the multiplicative compounding logic in the interest sub-section. Figure it Out Q7, section 1.3 p.19 (two buffaloes sold at different profit/loss percentages) is a good self-study challenge that surfaces the asymmetry of profit-base vs. loss-base.

periods.activity_title: Percentage Increase, Decrease, and Working Backwards

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q6, section 1.3 p.19
textbook_items_in_class.description: A number increased by 20% becomes 90. Find the original number.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q5, section 1.3 p.19
textbook_items_in_class.description: Rice price was ₹38/kg in 2024 and ₹42/kg in 2025. Find the rate of inflation (percentage increase in price).

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q8, section 1.3 p.20
textbook_items_in_class.description: Population of elephants increased by 5%. If last decade's population is p, which expression describes current population? (MCQ with options including p × 1.05.)

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q9, section 1.3 p.20
textbook_items_in_class.description: 'Demand for cameras has fallen by 85%.' Which statement(s) mean the same? (MCQ with six options involving 85%, 15%, 185% comparisons.)

homework.book_ref: Figure it Out Q7, section 1.3 p.19
homework.description: A milkman sold two buffaloes at ₹80,000 each — one at 5% profit and one at 10% loss. Find overall profit or loss.

time_bands.activity: Write on the board: 'After a 20% increase, a value becomes 90. What was the original?' Ask students to guess and check three candidate values before setting up any equation. This surfaces the working-backwards reasoning that the unit will formalise.

Students solve Figure it Out Q6, section 1.3 p.19 ("A number increased by 20% becomes 90....") using the proportional equation 1.2x = 90, so x = 75. Then solve Figure it Out Q5, section 1.3 p.19 ("Rice price ₹38/kg in 2024 and ₹42/kg in 2025. Find the rate of inflation....") using percentage increase = (42 − 38)/38 × 100. Both are discussed class-wide to confirm the direction of the computation (forward vs. backward).

Class works on Figure it Out Q8, section 1.3 p.20 ("Population of elephants increased by 5%; which expression describes current population?") as a group discussion. Elicit why the multiplier is 1.05 rather than 0.05 or 1 + 0.5. Then tackle Figure it Out Q9, section 1.3 p.20 ("Demand for cameras fallen by 85%; which statements mean the same?") — students match equivalent phrasings and explain why '15% of original' and 'fallen by 85%' convey the same relationship.

Students work in pairs to create their own 'working backwards' problem: they choose an original value, apply a percentage increase or decrease, and write the result — then swap with another pair to solve. At least two pairs present their problems and solutions.

Summarise the two directions of percentage reasoning: forward (apply the percentage to find the result) and backward (use the result and the percentage to find the original). Assign Figure it Out Q7, section 1.3 p.19 ("Two buffaloes sold at ₹80,000 each, one at 5% profit and one at 10% loss....") for home practice.

periods.teacher_notes: The most durable error here is treating 'increased by 20% to give 90' as 20% of 90, which gives the original as 72 instead of 75; the guess-and-check opening forces students to test their intuition before they reach for the formula. Figure it Out Q9 on camera demand is important for language precision — students should be able to translate freely among 'fallen by x%', 'is (100−x)% of original', and 'the new value is (100−x)% of the original'. Figure it Out Q6, section 1.3 p.19 (finding the original number) is a good self-study item for independent practice on the backward computation.

periods.activity_title: Simple and Compound Interest: Building the Formula Step by Step

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Example 7, section 1.3 p.21
textbook_items_in_class.description: ₹6000 deposited at 10% p.a. for 3 years. Option 1 (no compounding): interest returned each year, total = ₹7800. Option 2 (compounding): interest added back each year, total = ₹7986. Side-by-side tables build intuition.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Example 8, section 1.3 p.22
textbook_items_in_class.description: What % of the deposited amount is returned under each option? Without compounding: 7800/6000 × 100 = 130% (30% gain). With compounding: 7986/6000 × 100 = 133.1% (33.1% gain). Compounding expressed as 6000 × 1.1³.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Example 9, section 1.3 p.23
textbook_items_in_class.description: Generalises to principal p, rate r, time t. Without compounding: total = p(1 + rt). With compounding: total = p(1 + r)^t. Derivation shown step by step for both options.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 1.3 p.22
textbook_items_in_class.description: Bank of Yahapur: 10% p.a. Compare the return on ₹20,000 for 2 years with and without annual compounding.

homework.book_ref: Figure it Out Q5, section 1.3 p.23
homework.description: Post office: 7% p.a. Find interest on ₹50,000 for 3 years without compounding. How much more with compounding?

time_bands.activity: Pose the central question: you deposit ₹6000 at 10% per year for 3 years. Option A — interest is returned to you each year. Option B — interest is added to your deposit each year. Which earns more? Students estimate the final amounts for both options before any calculation.

Build the side-by-side table from Example 7, section 1.3 p.21 ("₹6000 at 10% p.a. for 3 years, with and without compounding....") year by year. Students fill in each row as the class progresses: Option 1 ends at ₹7800; Option 2 ends at ₹7986. Ask: in Option 2, why does the Year-2 interest differ from Year-1? Establish the key insight — the base grows each year because interest is reinvested.

Work through Example 8, section 1.3 p.22 ("What % of the deposited amount is returned under each option?") converting both totals to percentages of the principal: 130% vs 133.1%. Show that Option 2 equals 6000 × 1.1 × 1.1 × 1.1 = 6000 × 1.1³. Then derive the general formula in Example 9, section 1.3 p.23 ("Generalises: without compounding p(1+rt), with compounding p(1+r)^t....") step by step.

Students work individually on Figure it Out Q1, section 1.3 p.22 ("Bank of Yahapur: 10% p.a., ₹20,000 for 2 years, compare with and without compounding."). Two rows of computation; encourage students to use both the iterative approach and the formula, then confirm both agree.
Class confirms Q1 answers. Assign Figure it Out Q5, section 1.3 p.23 ("Post office: 7% p.a., ₹50,000 for 3 years....") as home practice to apply both formulas to a new principal and rate.

periods.teacher_notes: Students often add the interest rates rather than multiplying the multipliers — insisting on the year-by-year table first, before the formula, prevents this. Example 9, section 1.3 p.23 generalises elegantly from the concrete case; encourage students to re-derive the formula for 2 years before accepting the exponent notation for 3. Figure it Out Q2, section 1.3 p.22 (Bank of Wahapur, 5% for 4 years) is a good self-study item for additional formula practice.

periods.activity_title: Depreciation, Population Growth, and Compound Discounts

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Example 10, section 1.3 p.24
textbook_items_in_class.description: TV bought at ₹21,000; depreciates 5% after 1 year. Two equivalent methods: reduce by 5% (21000 − 1050 = ₹19,950) or multiply by 95% (0.95 × 21000 = ₹19,950).

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Example 11, section 1.3 p.24
textbook_items_in_class.description: Village population decreasing by 10% per decade from 1250. After 3 decades: 1250 × 0.9³ ≈ 911. Side-by-side: multiplicative vs. iterative subtraction approach. Rounds to ~910.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Example 12, section 1.3 p.26
textbook_items_in_class.description: Cakely offers 30% + 20% sequential discount vs. Cakify's flat 50%. On ₹200 cake: Cakely → ₹140 → ₹112 (44% total reduction); Cakify → ₹100 (50% reduction). Compounding of discounts means 30% + 20% < 50%.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q8, section 1.3 p.24
textbook_items_in_class.description: A city's population rises 3% every year. Current population is 1.5 crore. Find expected population after 3 years.

homework.book_ref: Figure it Out Q5, section 1.3 p.28
homework.description: Shopkeeper sets price with 35% profit margin, then offers 30% discount on selling price. Does he make a profit or a loss? Give reasons.

time_bands.activity: Introduce depreciation as 'negative compounding': a TV loses 5% of its value each year. Ask students to predict the value after 2 years — will the total loss be exactly 10%? Take predictions before computing.

Work through Example 10, section 1.3 p.24 ("TV bought at ₹21,000; depreciates 5%....") showing both methods — subtraction and multiplication by 0.95. Then extend to Example 11, section 1.3 p.24 ("Village population decreasing by 10% per decade from 1250....") using 1250 × 0.9³. Students see that the compound formula p(1+r)^t applies with r = −0.1, and compute the result both iteratively and with the exponent.

Work through Example 12, section 1.3 p.26 ("Cakely: 30% + 20% sequential discount; Cakify: flat 50%...."). Build the calculation: ₹200 → 70% of 200 = ₹140 → 80% of 140 = ₹112 (effective 44% off). Cakify gives ₹100 (50% off). Ask students: why doesn't 30 + 20 = 50? Formalise: the second discount acts on an already-reduced price, so the total reduction is always less than the sum of the two rates.

Students work individually on Figure it Out Q8, section 1.3 p.24 ("A city's population rises 3% every year, current population 1.5 crore. Find expected population after 3 years.") using the compound formula. Students write 1.5 × 1.03³ and compute step by step.

Class confirms Q8 answer. Assign Figure it Out Q5, section 1.3 p.28 ("Shopkeeper: 35% profit margin, then 30% discount on SP. Profit or loss?") as home practice — this requires chaining the two multiplicative adjustments, directly applying the compound-discount logic from Example 12.

periods.teacher_notes: Students frequently claim that two sequential discounts of 30% and 20% equal a flat 50% discount; Example 12, section 1.3 p.26 is precisely the place to break this belief — compute both numerically before generalising. For depreciation, confirm that students write the multiplier as (1 − rate), not (1 + rate), which gives growth; a sign error here produces absurdly large values. Example 13, section 1.3 p.27 (Surbhi's 50% markup then 50% discount yielding a 25% loss) is an excellent self-study counterintuitive problem.

periods.activity_title: Tricky Percentages, Algebraic Generalisation, and Real-World Puzzles

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Example 13, section 1.3 p.27
textbook_items_in_class.description: Surbhi marks goods at 50% profit margin (1.5x), then offers 50% discount (0.75x). Results in 25% loss, not break-even. Derives the correct discount for break-even: 33.33%. Bar model illustrates the three price levels.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q7, section 1.3 p.28
textbook_items_in_class.description: Explore: 5% of 40 = 40% of 5; 25% of 12 = 12% of 25; 15% of 60 = 60% of 15. Generalise: is x% of y always equal to y% of x? Justify algebraically.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q10, section 1.3 p.29
textbook_items_in_class.description: Bus fares increased 3% last year and 4% this year. Find overall percentage price increase over 2 years.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q14, section 1.3 p.30
textbook_items_in_class.description: Try This: 100 people, 99% left-handed. How many left-handed people must leave to bring the percentage down to 98%?

time_bands.activity: Open with the Surbhi puzzle from Example 13, section 1.3 p.27 ("Surbhi marks goods at 50% profit margin, then offers 50% discount...."). Ask students to predict whether she breaks even, makes a profit, or makes a loss. After predictions, work through the bar model: cost price x, marked price 1.5x, selling price 0.5 × 1.5x = 0.75x — a 25% loss. Ask: what discount should she offer to break even? Students attempt this before the answer (33.33%) is revealed.

Students investigate Figure it Out Q7, section 1.3 p.28 ("5% of 40 = 40% of 5; 25% of 12 = 12% of 25; generalise: is x% of y always equal to y% of x?"). Pairs first verify the numerical examples, then construct the algebraic argument: x/100 × y = y/100 × x. Whole-class share of the algebra; discuss why this commutativity is surprising to intuition but trivial in symbols.

Class tackles Figure it Out Q10, section 1.3 p.29 ("Bus fares increased 3% last year and 4% this year. Find overall percentage price increase over 2 years."). Students apply the compound formula: overall multiplier = 1.03 × 1.04 = 1.0712, so 7.12% increase — not 7%. Contrast with the intuitive (wrong) answer of 3 + 4 = 7.

Students work on Figure it Out Q14, section 1.3 p.30 ("100 people, 99% left-handed. How many left-handed people must leave to bring the percentage down to 98%?"). This is deliberately counter-intuitive: 99 left-handed out of 100 total; removing 50 left-handers gives 49 out of 50 = 98%. Students check by substitution. Discuss: why does removing just one person not work?

Close the unit with a whole-class reflection: name one thing in this chapter that surprised you about percentages. Take three or four responses. Remind students that the chapter's exercises contain many further challenges — Figure it Out Q13, section 1.3 p.29 (shop deals comparison) is one particularly rich puzzle to explore independently.

periods.teacher_notes: The Surbhi example is a powerful closing provocation because it defeats a nearly universal intuition (50% up then 50% down = same); insist students set up the bar model or algebraic chain rather than relying on verbal reasoning alone. Figure it Out Q14 is similarly counter-intuitive — the answer of 50 feels impossibly large; guide students to verify by substituting back into the definition of percentage. Figure it Out Q13, section 1.3 p.29 (three shop deals, effective discount comparison) is an excellent self-study extension for students who want to continue exploring the multiplicative logic of compound discounts.

items.prompt: A percentage is best defined as a fraction whose denominator is:

teacher_guide.expected_answer: B — 100. A percentage expresses a quantity as a fraction with denominator 100; 'per cent' comes from the Latin per centum, meaning out of a hundred.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Recall the definition: percentage = fraction over 100, so the denominator is always 100.

what_each_option_reveals.A: The student may be confusing percentage with the decimal-tenths place, where the denominator is 10.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The student may be conflating percentage with parts per thousand (‰) or thinking of the decimal-thousandths place.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student has not grasped the fixed-denominator definition and may think the denominator always equals the numerator (i.e., 100%).

inclusivity.support: Invite the student to re-read the opening definition in section 1.1 and write out 75% as a fraction before choosing.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask the student to write three equivalent forms for 35% — as a fraction, a decimal, and a ratio — and explain why all three represent the same quantity.

items.prompt: In a class of 80 students, 36 travel to school by bicycle. What percentage of the students travel by bicycle? Show your working.

teacher_guide.method_one_line: Write the given count as a fraction of the whole, then multiply by 100 using the equivalent-fraction or cross-multiplication method from section 1.1.

inclusivity.support: Encourage the student to draw a bar divided into 80 equal parts, shade 36, and ask how many parts would be shaded if the bar had 100 parts instead.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask the student to solve the same problem using two different methods (equivalent-fraction scaling and cross-multiplication) and confirm both give 45%.

exercise.description: 15 of 80 students come to school by walking. What percentage come by walking?

items.prompt: A fruit drink contains 15% real juice. If a bottle holds 340 ml of the drink, how many millilitres are real juice?

teacher_guide.method_one_line: Apply the formula y% of quantity = (y/100) × quantity, with y = 15 and quantity = 340 ml.

inclusivity.support: Prompt the student to first find 10% of 340 ml (34 ml) mentally, then find 5% (17 ml) and add the two results.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask: if the bottle size changes to 500 ml but the juice percentage stays the same, find the new juice volume — and then ask what percentage of the original 51 ml this new amount represents.

items.prompt: Without calculating exactly, which of the following is the largest?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: B — 37% of 280 = 103.6. The others: A = 100, C = 100, D = 90. So B is the largest.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Estimate each using benchmark percentages (50% of 200 = 100; 25% of 400 = 100; 10% of 900 = 90; 37% of 280 > 36% of 280 = 100.8), confirming B exceeds the others.

what_each_option_reveals.D: The student may have correctly computed 50% of 200 = 100 but not compared it carefully with 37% of 280.
what_each_option_reveals.B: The student may recognise 25% of 400 = 100 but failed to compare this with 37% of 280, which exceeds 100.
what_each_option_reveals.A: The student may have focused on the largest base (900) without realising that 10% of 900 is only 90, less than the others.

inclusivity.support: Suggest the student first find 10% of each value to get anchor amounts, then scale up to the given percentage.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask the student to rank all four from smallest to largest and justify each ranking step with a one-sentence estimation argument.

items.prompt: 45% of a number is 108. Find 120% of the same number. Show your working.

teacher_guide.method_one_line: Use the scaling relationship: find 1% (or 100%) from the given percentage, then scale to 120% by multiplying.

inclusivity.support: Draw a percentage bar: mark 45% = 108, find 9% = 108/5 = 21.6, then build up to 100% and 120% in steps.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask the student to also find 9% and 18% of the same number, explaining each scaling step, as in the Fill-in-the-blanks pattern of Figure it Out Q5.

items.prompt: A shopkeeper buys a pen for ₹40 and sells it for ₹52. Find the percentage profit on the cost price. Show your working.

teacher_guide.method_one_line: Compute profit as SP − CP, then apply percentage profit = (profit ÷ CP) × 100, consistent with the method in section 1.3's profit-loss examples.

inclusivity.support: Remind the student that profit percentage is always computed on the cost price — write the formula (profit ÷ CP) × 100 and ask them to substitute.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask: at what selling price would the profit percentage be exactly 45%? Set up and solve the equation SP = 1.45 × 40.

items.prompt: After a 25% increase, a value becomes 175. What was the original value? Show your working.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: The original value is 140. Working: 1.25 × original = 175, so original = 175 ÷ 1.25 = 140.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Set up the equation (1 + 0.25) × x = 175 and solve by dividing both sides by 1.25, using the backward-percentage reasoning from section 1.3.

inclusivity.support: Suggest finding 25% of 175 and subtracting — then verify: does 140 × 1.25 = 175?
inclusivity.challenge: Ask: if the value then decreases by 25%, what is the final value, and is it equal to the original 140? Explain why or why not.

items.prompt: Priya deposits ₹8,000 in a bank at 10% per annum. Compare the total amount she receives after 2 years (a) without compounding (interest is returned each year) and (b) with annual compounding (interest is added back each year). Show your working for both.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: (a) Without compounding: interest each year = 10% of 8000 = ₹800; total after 2 years = 8000 + 800 + 800 = ₹9,600. (b) With compounding: after Year 1 amount = 8000 × 1.1 = ₹8,800; after Year 2 amount = 8800 × 1.1 = ₹9,680. So with compounding she receives ₹9,680, which is ₹80 more than without compounding.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Without compounding use p(1 + rt) = 8000 × (1 + 0.1 × 2) = 9600; with compounding use p(1+r)^t = 8000 × 1.1² = 9680.

inclusivity.support: Draw a two-row year-by-year table (as in Example 7, section 1.3 p.21) and fill in each year's starting amount and interest separately for the two options.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask: how does the difference between the two options change for 3 years instead of 2? Extend the table and generalise in words.

items.prompt: A town's population is currently 4,00,000 and grows at 5% per year. Using the compound growth formula, find the expected population after 2 years. Show your working.

teacher_guide.method_one_line: Apply the compound growth formula p(1 + r)^t with p = 4,00,000, r = 0.05, t = 2.

inclusivity.support: Compute year by year: after Year 1 = 4,00,000 × 1.05 = 4,20,000; after Year 2 = 4,20,000 × 1.05 = 4,41,000.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask: if the growth rate changes to 3% in Year 1 and 4% in Year 2, find the population after 2 years and compare it with the uniform-5% result.

items.prompt: A store offers a sequential discount of 20% followed by 10% on the original price of ₹500. A competitor offers a flat 30% discount on the same item. Without calculating, predict which deal is better for the customer, and then verify by computing both final prices.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: The flat 30% discount is better. Flat 30%: 500 × 0.7 = ₹350. Sequential 20% + 10%: 500 × 0.8 = ₹400, then 400 × 0.9 = ₹360. The flat deal gives ₹350, which is ₹10 cheaper.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: For sequential discounts multiply the two retention multipliers (0.8 × 0.9 = 0.72, so 28% effective reduction); flat 30% gives 30% reduction — 30% > 28%, so the flat deal is better.

inclusivity.support: Use the method from Example 12, section 1.3 p.26: draw two arrow steps for the sequential discount to make each multiplication visible before comparing.
inclusivity.challenge: Find the single equivalent discount percentage for the 20% + 10% deal and explain algebraically why it equals 1 − (0.8 × 0.9) = 28%, not 30%.
